source.version: Undated preprint with Supplementary Materials; the title page states that the manuscript has not been peer-reviewed (PDF p. 1). No version number or manuscript date is shown, and retrieval.json provides no version_saved.
source.title_on_document: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Human Creativity Through Real-Time Evaluative Feedback

supplement.where: Supplementary Materials, PDF pp. 39-52; supporting text on pp. 40-42 and Tables S1-S9 on pp. 43-51. Materials, data, and scripts are also linked at https://osf.io/6k52d/?view_only=398df4fd924440ee9387af4f6434d422 (PDF pp. 2, 15).
supplement.holds: Model-training and validation details; invalid-response screening; analyzed-sample demographics (Table S1); participant-level self-rating/originality correlations (Tables S2 and S5); full originality mixed-model coefficients and standard errors (Tables S3 and S6); mediation coefficients and confidence intervals (Tables S4 and S7); and alternative evaluation-accuracy analyses (Tables S8 and S9). The full model coefficient tables are included in this PDF. Cluster-robust sensitivity estimates are described as unreported (PDF p. 18, Analysis strategy).

paper_design_summary: Study 1 compared continuous GPT-3 originality feedback, feedback during practice only, and no feedback while an online sample generated solutions to design problems; the final dataset contains 554 adults, but random assignment to feedback conditions is not stated (PDF pp. 8-11, 16). Study 2 randomly assigned museum visitors to immediate or delayed AuDrA feedback while completing drawings and reports 36,198 people in its final dataset (PDF pp. 12-17). Both studies scored human-produced outputs with the models supplying numerical feedback; Study 1 also measures unassisted originality after practice-only feedback, and neither intervention supplies creative ideas (PDF pp. 9-14, 20, 31).

studies.label: Study 1: online design-problem experiment with numerical GPT-3 feedback

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants received continuous feedback, intermediate feedback during practice only, or no feedback. The document explicitly randomizes the sequence of design problems, but does not explicitly randomize people to the feedback conditions. Design class other preserves this uncertainty rather than asserting either randomized or non-random assignment.
assignment.quote: Condition was a between-participants factor with three levels (continuous feedback, intermediate feedback, no feedback).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 9), Procedure; PDF p. 12, Figure 2.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF pp. 2 and 15, Open access statement / Transparency and openness: https://aspredicted.org/bgmj-yrm4.pdf. PDF p. 15 reports deviations including the added intermediate condition, changed evaluation-accuracy analysis, and inclusion of engineers and non-engineers. The linked preregistration could not be retrieved because network access was denied.

arms.name: Continuous feedback
arms.description: GPT-3 numerical originality feedback during practice and all scored design-problem trials; all groups also received repeated be-creative reminders. The pre-exclusion procedure reports 208 participants receiving this condition, but neither random assignment nor an unambiguous analyzed arm total is supplied (PDF p. 11; subgroup counts on p. 16). The generative_ai code identifies the GPT-3 model family; its numeric-only evaluative use remains a scope question.

arms.name: Intermediate feedback (practice only)
arms.description: GPT-3 numerical originality feedback during practice, with no feedback during scored trials. The procedure reports 214 participants receiving this condition before exclusions; random assignment and a reliable analyzed arm total are not stated (PDF p. 11; subgroup counts on p. 16).

arms.name: No feedback (control)
arms.description: No feedback during practice or scored trials; the same repeated be-creative reminders as the feedback groups. The procedure reports 208 participants before exclusions; random assignment and a reliable analyzed arm total are not stated (PDF p. 11; subgroup counts on p. 16).

participants.exclusions: Recruited: 629 adults (PDF p. 8). Invalid ideas, less than 1% of 8,173 initial entries, were removed after automated screening and human review; 11 participants were excluded for completion times more than three standard deviations from the average; 56 were identified with more than 25% of responses showing copy-and-paste behavior; 15 used a mobile phone/tablet; and 34 trials containing only one response were excluded (PDF pp. 15-16). The final dataset is explicitly 554 adults and 7,174 valid responses (p. 16). Overlap among participant exclusions is not stated. Arm totals remain null: the procedure counts conflict with the overall recruitment total, and p. 16 reports 327 engineers and 228 non-engineers whereas Table S1 reports 327 and 227 (PDF p. 43).
participants.who: English-speaking adults recruited through Prolific, including participants with and without engineering experience (PDF p. 8).
participants.country: United States, Canada, and United Kingdom (PDF p. 8).
participants.quote: The final dataset comprised 554 adults aged between 18 and 71 years
participants.locator: PDF p. 16 (printed p. 14), Data cleaning; recruitment on PDF p. 8; exclusions on pp. 15-16; Table S1 on p. 43.

ai_tool.how_used: Numerical evaluation of participants' own ideas, returned through an API after each submission. Scores were normalized to a 1-10 feedback scale and displayed graphically; the model provided no ideas or qualitative suggestions (PDF pp. 9-11, 31). The supplementary text identifies davinci-002 and a formatted problem/solution/rating completion used for fine-tuning (PDF p. 40). This is a generative language-model architecture used only as an originality scorer; whether such numerical feedback meets the atlas intervention scope is unresolved.

task.description: Generate creative solutions to improving clean-water access in remote areas, helping people with memory impairments remember tasks, and improving pedestrian-crossing safety. An unanalyzed practice problem asked for three solutions to improving remote learning. Up to 10 ideas were allowed for each scored problem (PDF pp. 8-9).
task.duration: 6 minutes per design problem (PDF p. 9); mean duration of the full study 33.62 minutes (PDF p. 11).

outcomes.name: Originality of design solutions with continuous feedback
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-3 originality scores on a 1-10 scale, recorded as ideas were submitted (PDF pp. 9-10, 20). The same scoring model supplied the feedback. Originality is analyzed per response, with participant and problem random intercepts, rather than as participant means (PDF pp. 16-18). The 7,174 observations are the common model dataset across all three arms, not the size of either pairwise contrast (PDF p. 16). Model 1 tests condition alone; Models 2 and 3 add response/trial order and self-ratings respectively and are variants of this same outcome (Table S3, PDF p. 45). Originality is tied to the paper's primary hypothesis on PDF p. 21. S1-O2 separates the practice-only contrast because scored production occurs after feedback removal.
outcomes.delay: Same session, with feedback continuing through the scored trials in the continuous-feedback arm (PDF p. 11).

contrasts.reported: Continuous feedback: EMM = 6.67, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [6.34, 7.00]; control: EMM = 6.13, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [5.79, 6.46]; t(8.50) = −3.56, p < .01; d = −0.35, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [−0.57, −0.13]. Table S3, condition (feedback): Model 1 b = 0.54 (SE = 0.15), p < .001; Model 2 b = 0.66 (SE = 0.20), p < .001; Model 3 b = 0.12 (SE = 0.24), p = .62. Negative d and t are preserved as printed; the feedback arm has the higher EMM. Model 3 adjusts for self-ratings and is a mechanism analysis, not a separate creativity outcome.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22 (printed p. 20), Figure 3 caption and Does feedback drive changes in originality?; PDF p. 45 (printed supplementary p. 13), Table S3.

contrasts.reported: Continuous feedback: EMM = 6.67, SE = 0.15; intermediate feedback: EMM = 6.80, SE = 0.15; d = 0.08, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.30]; t(3.80) = −0.86, p = .68. These signs and statistics are reproduced as printed. The treatment arm continues feedback during production; the comparison arm has feedback removed after practice.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22 (printed p. 20), Figure 3 caption and Does feedback drive changes in originality?; intervention timing on PDF p. 11.

outcomes.name: Originality of unassisted design solutions after practice-only feedback
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same GPT-3 originality metric and common response-level mixed models as S1-O1, but the intermediate-feedback group receives no feedback while producing the scored solutions (PDF pp. 9-11, 16-18, 20). AI remains an unseen outcome scorer; this does not make AI assistance available to participants in the test phase. The 7,174 observations are shared across the full three-arm model, not the number of outputs in this two-arm contrast (PDF p. 16). Model variants are grouped here; Table S3 supplies the intermediate-versus-control coefficients (PDF p. 45).
outcomes.delay: Same session following practice; no elapsed interval is stated. Feedback is removed before the scored design-problem trials (PDF p. 11).

contrasts.reported: Intermediate feedback: EMM = 6.80, SE = 0.15, [6.46, 7.13]; control: EMM = 6.13, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [5.79, 6.46]; t(8.95) = −4.36, p < .01; d = −0.43, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [−0.66, −0.21]. Table S3, condition (intermediate): Model 1 b = 0.67 (SE = 0.15), p < .001; Model 2 b = 1.06 (SE = 0.21), p < .001; Model 3 b = 0.92 (SE = 0.24), p < .001. Negative d and t are preserved as printed; intermediate feedback has the higher EMM.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22 (printed p. 20), Does feedback drive changes in originality?; PDF p. 45 (printed supplementary p. 13), Table S3; feedback removal documented on PDF p. 11.

studies.label: Study 2: museum drawing experiment with AuDrA feedback

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual museum visitors were assigned after a warm-up to immediate feedback after the first drawing or delayed feedback after two drawings. Subsequent drawings could receive feedback in both conditions; the primary analysis focuses on the first two drawings per shape (PDF pp. 14, 17).
assignment.quote: participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: immediate or delayed feedback.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 15, Transparency and openness, explicitly states that Study 2 was not preregistered. Table S9 is nonetheless headed (Preregistered analysis) on PDF p. 51; the explicit study-level statement is used here.

arms.name: Immediate feedback
arms.description: AuDrA numerical originality feedback after the first drawing, before production of the second. Coded other_aid because the identified AuDrA model is a convolutional neural network for scoring drawings, not an image generator. Assigned and analyzed counts are printed on PDF pp. 14 and 16.

arms.name: Delayed feedback (control for second drawing)
arms.description: AuDrA feedback begins after two drawings; the second drawing is produced before any feedback for that shape. Both conditions can receive feedback on later drawings. This is a no-feedback comparator during the primary scored phase, within a delayed-feedback arm (PDF pp. 14, 17, 47).

participants.exclusions: The initial total is 37,823 visitors (PDF p. 12), with assignment counts reported on p. 14. Drawings in the bottom 3% of completion times were excluded: 2,632 entries submitted in 6 seconds or less (PDF p. 16). The final dataset contains 36,198 people and 77,142 drawings, with 18,136 analyzed in immediate feedback and 18,062 in delayed feedback (p. 16). The number of people removed specifically by each exclusion is not stated. Analysis was restricted to the first two drawings per shape (p. 17); the number of people contributing a second drawing and the exact resulting model observation count are not separately reported.
participants.who: Science-museum visitors, including children with parent/guardian consent, participating in a Living Lab exhibit (PDF pp. 12-14).
participants.country: Poland (museum location; participant nationality not stated), PDF pp. 12-14.
participants.locator: PDF p. 16 (printed p. 14), Data cleaning; initial total on p. 12; random assignment and arm allocation counts on p. 14; analysis restriction on p. 17.

ai_tool.how_used: Predicts originality of submitted drawings and displays numerical feedback beside participants' own ratings (PDF p. 13). The Discussion explicitly identifies the model as a previously trained convolutional neural network (PDF p. 29). Although p. 13 also calls the scorer a fine-tuned large language model, the named system and the Discussion identify AuDrA, not a generative drawing tool. Feedback is numerical only (PDF p. 31); no generated image, idea, or qualitative suggestion is supplied.

task.description: Complete simple unfinished shapes to create something new and interesting on a touchscreen, using six possible shapes after a distinct warm-up task. Participants could make repeated drawings and choose further shapes; the main comparison uses the first two drawings per shape (PDF pp. 12-14, 17).
task.duration: No time constraints for individual drawings (PDF p. 13). Recruitment took place from June 2023 to June 2024 (PDF pp. 12-13).

outcomes.name: Drawing originality, principally the second drawing after immediate versus delayed feedback
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: AuDrA originality score, reported as ranging from 0 to 10 (PDF p. 20). The main contrast is the second drawing: the immediate group has received feedback, while the delayed group has not; the first drawing is baseline and later drawings in both groups may receive feedback (PDF p. 17). The feedback system remains in use, so this is not an after_ai withdrawal outcome. The pooled first/second-drawing analysis and models adding response/trial order or self-ratings are variants of the same metric (PDF pp. 23-24; Table S6, p. 48). Analysis uses output-level scores with participant and shape random intercepts (PDF pp. 16-18). The paper reports 77,142 drawings in the cleaned dataset but does not separately state the observation count for the first-two-per-shape restriction or the second-drawing contrast, so n_units is null. This answers the feedback-with-AI question descriptively, but AuDrA does not establish a generative-AI intervention.
outcomes.delay: Same session; immediate-arm participants see feedback on their first drawing before making the second (PDF pp. 14, 17). The word delayed in the control-arm name does not denote a later outcome session.

contrasts.reported: Primary second-drawing contrast: immediate feedback EMM = 4.84, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.79, 4.90]; delayed-feedback control EMM = 4.44, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.40, 4.48]; t(54,419) = −11.83, p < .001; d = −0.20, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [−0.24, −0.17] (PDF p. 24). Baseline first drawing: feedback EMM = 4.63, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.60, 4.67]; control EMM = 4.62, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.59, 4.66]; t(46,652) = −0.50, p = .62 (p. 24). The analysis including both first and second drawings reports feedback EMM = 4.65, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.62, 4.68], versus control EMM = 4.49, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.46, 4.52]; t(29,398) = −7.25, p < .001; d = −0.08, SE = 0.01, 95% CI [−0.10, −0.06] (p. 23). Table S6: Model 1 condition b = 0.16 (SE = 0.02), p < .001; Model 2 Response order × Condition b = 0.41 (SE = 0.03), p < .001 (p. 48). Negative d and t values are reproduced as printed, while the immediate-feedback condition has the higher post-feedback EMM. ai_vs_bau describes the absence of feedback in the control arm before its second drawing; the randomized arms differ in feedback timing.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22, Figure 3 caption; PDF pp. 23-24 (printed pp. 21-22), Does feedback drive changes in originality?; PDF p. 48 (printed supplementary p. 16), Table S6; phase-specific control definition on PDF pp. 17 and 47 (Table S5 notes).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Not stated for either intervention sample. Study 1 reuses an existing corpus to train the scoring model, and Study 2 uses the previously trained AuDrA model; neither is described as a reanalysis of another paper's intervention participants.
sample_overlap.quote: The model was trained specifically for this study using an existing sample of design ideas
sample_overlap.locator: PDF p. 9, Development of AI feedback; PDF p. 29, Discussion; PDF p. 40, Supporting text.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement is reported. Listed affiliations are universities and a science centre, funding is from public research agencies, and the authors declare no conflicts of interest. Use of GPT-3 is reported as a study tool, without a stated company role.
company_involvement.locator: PDF pp. 1-2, affiliations and Author Note; GPT-3 use on PDF p. 9.

eligibility.reason: Study 1 analyzes 554 people and scores the originality of their produced ideas, satisfying the size and output criteria (PDF pp. 9, 16, 20-22), but the document does not explicitly state random assignment to feedback conditions: only problem order is randomized (PDF p. 11; Figure 2 on p. 12). Its fine-tuned GPT-3 davinci-002 provides numerical evaluations only (PDF pp. 9-10, 31, 40), leaving a scope question about including evaluative-only use of a generative language model. Study 2 explicitly randomizes people (PDF p. 14), analyzes 36,198 participants (p. 16), and scores drawings (pp. 13, 24), but its identified AuDrA convolutional network is a predictive scoring system rather than generative AI (p. 29), so Study 2 alone cannot establish core eligibility. No study is a comparison of AI-generated versus human-generated output, and uncertain assignment in Study 1 is not evidence of non-random assignment. Study 1 is the potentially relevant generative-model study and is conservatively classified other pending assignment and scope confirmation.

one_line_finding: Feedback groups had higher model-scored originality: Study 1 EMM 6.67 with continuous feedback and 6.80 with practice-only feedback versus 6.13 in control (PDF p. 22), and Study 2 second-drawing EMM 4.84 with immediate versus 4.44 with delayed feedback (PDF p. 24).
open_questions: Was allocation of Study 1 participants to feedback conditions randomized? The PDF describes random problem order only (p. 11); the preregistration linked on pp. 2 and 15 could not be accessed.

Does the atlas include a generative language model used solely to return numerical originality ratings? Study 1 uses GPT-3 davinci-002 (PDF pp. 9, 40), while both interventions provide numeric-only feedback (p. 31). Study 2 instead identifies AuDrA as a convolutional neural network (p. 29), despite contradictory large-language-model wording on p. 13.

What are the correct Study 1 allocation and analyzed arm totals? Recruitment is 629 (PDF p. 8), while procedure counts are 208 continuous, 214 intermediate, and 208 control (p. 11). The analyzed dataset is 554, but p. 16 reports 327 engineers and 228 non-engineers; Table S1 instead reports 327 and 227 (p. 43). The subgroup counts on p. 16 are 114/106/107 engineers and 76/75/77 non-engineers for continuous/intermediate/control. No conflicting count has been silently repaired.

How many drawings and people contribute to the Study 2 second-drawing contrast? The PDF reports 77,142 drawings from 36,198 people in the cleaned dataset (p. 16), then restricts analyses to the first two drawings per shape without a separate model or second-drawing sample count (p. 17).

Which human-rating sample descriptions are correct? Study 1 model development reports 20 expert raters (PDF pp. 9, 40), whereas the Discussion says 40 (p. 29). Study 2 validation reports 141 raters (pp. 13, 40), whereas the Discussion says 120 (p. 29). These raters are not added to intervention participant counts.
notes: Screened by A on 2026-10-09. All paper locators use one-based physical PDF pages; printed page numbers are supplied selectively because pagination restarts before the references. The entire markdown, including references and Supplementary Materials, was read; cited design/count/statistic pages were checked using PyMuPDF text extraction, and Figure 2 was also inspected. S1-O1 and S1-O2 are the same originality metric separated to preserve with_ai versus after_ai timing; their common model observation count must not be added. Self-ratings, metacognitive evaluation accuracy, and mediation mechanisms are not additional creative-output outcomes; self-evaluation correlations and accuracy tables are supplementary mechanism evidence (PDF pp. 18-19, 24-28; Tables S2, S4-S5, S7-S9 on pp. 44, 46-47, 49-51). No fluency, usefulness, flexibility, or across-person diversity treatment outcome is reported. Human ratings used to train or validate the models are not separate AI-assistance studies. Reported standardized effects and their signs were transcribed without calculating, correcting, or reversing any effect size; treatment_higher refers to higher originality in the treatment arm. Analyzed arm means/SDs/counts are not supplied as a complete extractable set. Study 1 allocation and analyzed arm counts remain null rather than being inferred from inconsistent subgroup totals. Network attempts to the named AsPredicted preregistration and the named OSF repository both failed with Windows socket-permission errors; no external contents were used. The data/code link is documented on PDF pp. 2 and 15.
